question: Biomethane is increasingly being used in Germany as liquid fuel (known as bio-LNG) for heavy goods vehicles. The Renewable Energy Directive (RED II) has introduced incentives for this. Liquefaction plants have recently been built to process regionally produced biomethane into bio-LNG.

However, so-called ‘virtual liquefaction pathway models’, in which fossil LNG is declared as bio-LNG with biomethane certificates without actually liquefying biomethane are becoming standard practice in the EU. The RED Directive allows this form of purely accounting-based relabelling, even though it conceals emissions and acts as a disincentive for physically lowemission production pathways.

The delegated act under Article 31(5) of RED II provides for the possibility of closing this loophole by adjusting emission values or making clarifications to methodology. According to industry figures, investments of around EUR 300 million in innovative bio-LNG plants in Germany alone depend on this decision. 1.
When does the Commission intend to publish the announced delegated act revising Annexes V and VI to Directive (EU) 2018/2001, and reviewing in particular ‘virtual liquefaction pathway models’?

Does the Commission agree that the virtual liquefaction of biomethane is does not capture enough international fossil emissions upstream and that this puts bio-LNG produced in Europe at a disadvantage?
How will the Commission ensure that low-emission production pathways are not disadvantaged vis-à-vis purely accounting-based constructions in future emissions strategies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.11.2025) The Commission is currently preparing the update of Annexes V and VI to the Renewable Energy Directive1 and it is expected to publish the draft for public feedback in the coming months. Liquefaction will be covered with the update.

The Union Database will allow the traceability of both physical and virtual liquefaction, allowing for the registration of all accumulated greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions values related to the liquefaction process. This approach aims to prevent discrimination against EU facilities using physical liquefaction related to concerns on emission capture and equal footing for bio-liquefied natural gas (LNG) producers.

The conversion factors and comprehensive greenhouse gas emissions accounting methodology stipulated in Annexes V and VI together with Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/9962 on sustainability certification and the Union Database will ensure that there will be no discrimination. This approach also ensures the fair treatment across different liquefaction methods within the EU.

In addition, bio-LNG in the FuelEU Maritime Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/18053) plays a significant role in supporting the decarbonisation of the maritime sector, subject to strict conditions. The Commission has explicitly provided a framework for how bio-LNG is treated under the FuelEU Maritime Regulation.
Well to wake emissions are taken into account and this benefits low-emission production pathways, compared to synthetic fuels or fossil LNG with minimal GHG savings.
